After breakfast, you’ll take a sightseeing tour of Cuenca.

The historic center was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List on December 1, 1999. The city preserves historic monuments, museums, old churches, cobbled streets and houses with Republican-era façades. Among its most striking buildings is the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, one of the largest cathedrals in the Americas.

Cuenca is also known as the “Basin of the Andes” and the “Athens of Ecuador.” The tour touches on the city’s connections with several Ecuadorian poets and historical figures.

You’ll see the Flower Market Square, the cathedral, Abdón Calderón Square and the Turi viewpoint. You’ll also visit traditional galleries and a factory that makes the hats known as Panama hats. Despite their name, these hats are made in Ecuador. At the artisan stalls, you can buy alpaca wool goods and silver jewelry.

The day’s main stops include the hat factory, the viewpoint, the main square, the cathedral, San Francisco Square, the artisan market, the fruit market and the riverfront.

Accommodation at the four-star El Dorado.

Breakfast is included.
Blue cathedral domes and turrets above a red-brick façade in Cuenca, Ecuador
Cuenca, Ecuador: the cathedral’s blue domes against a gray sky

After breakfast, visit Cajas National Park, about 30 km west of Cuenca. The park covers 28,544 hectares and contains more than 250 small lakes. It was designated a national park on November 5, 1996.

The landscape combines valleys, lakes, rocky outcrops and páramo. A thick cover of grass and cushion plants helps retain water. Tres Cruces, the highest point on the route accessible by road, sits on the watershed. Some rivers flow toward the Pacific Ocean, while others drain into the Atlantic basin.

The weather is cool, windy and rainy. In the forests and highlands, you may see birds such as hummingbirds and gray-breasted mountain toucans.

In the afternoon, you set out for Guayaquil. The drive takes about three and a half hours, with a stop at a cacao-growing hacienda. Cacao is an important crop in Ecuador’s Pacific region. The hacienda covers about 15 hectares in an area of tropical dry forest.

On the tour, you’ll learn how the land is prepared, how cacao is grown and harvested, and how the crop is prepared for export. In harvest season, you can watch the producers at work. Lunch at the hacienda is included. There’s also a hands-on session where you can make chocolate paste, brew hot chocolate and taste it.

After the tour, continue to Guayaquil.

Accommodation at the four-star Palace.

Breakfast and lunch are included.
